title: Phrasal verbs: turn it on, look after it
tagline: Some phrasal verbs split around the object (turn it on), others never do (look after it).
why: Phrasal verbs are everywhere in everyday English: put on a coat, pick up a bag, find out the answer. B1 Preliminary tests them in the multiple-choice cloze, and the Speaking and Writing tasks sound more natural with them. The biggest problem for students is where the object goes: turn it on is correct, but turn on it is not.

hook.text: Miss Vega: "Please turn the lights on." Liam: "I turned them on, Miss." Sofia: "I'm looking for my pen — did you pick it up?" Nadia: "Yes, I'm looking after it for you."
hook.ask: Where do the words them and it go: before or after the little word on and up? And does looking after it work like turn them on?

diagrams.title: Where does the object go?
diagrams.caption: With a pronoun (it, them, him, her) a separable phrasal verb always splits: turn it on, never turn on it.

rows.label: With a noun
cells: turn the light on / turn on the light

rows.label: Other examples
cells: put on, take off, pick up, give up
look for, get on with, look after

head: Type
Rule
Example
rows: noun goes in the middle or after; pronoun always in the middle
object always comes after the whole phrasal verb
I look after my brother. / I look after him.

verb + two small words, never split

use.point: Separable phrasal verbs with a noun: two possible positions

examples.note: noun in the middle, same meaning

examples.text: Mateo picked up the ball and ran.
examples.note: pick up = lift from the floor

use.point: Separable phrasal verbs with a pronoun: always in the middle

examples.note: it goes between put and on
them goes between take and off

examples.text: I dropped my pen and Liam picked it up.

use.point: Inseparable phrasal verbs: never split them

examples.text: I get on with everyone in my class.
examples.note: get on with = have a good relationship

examples.text: I get up at six on school days.
Don't give up! You can do it.

watch_out.why: With a pronoun (it, them, him), a separable phrasal verb must split.

watch_out.wrong: Take off them before you come in.
watch_out.right: Take them off before you come in.
watch_out.why: The pronoun goes between take and off.

watch_out.wrong: She looks the baby after every day.
watch_out.right: She looks after the baby every day.
watch_out.why: Look after is inseparable: never put the object inside.
Look for is inseparable too: the object comes after for.

watch_out.wrong: I get on well with he.
watch_out.why: After with, use the object pronoun: him, her, them.
Give up is separable, so the pronoun goes in the middle.

l1.why: In Spanish the pronoun is attached to the verb. In English it goes between the verb and the particle.
Spanish cuidar is one verb. English often needs a phrasal verb: look after.
Spanish buscar has no small word. English needs look for to try to find something.

l1.es: Me llevo bien con mis primos.
l1.wrong: I take well with my cousins.
l1.why: Spanish llevarse bien is get on with in English, never take well.

remember.trick: It in the middle, but look AFTER it!
remember.tip: Pronouns (it, them) go in the middle for turn on, take off, pick up. For look after, look for and get on with, nothing goes in the middle.

dialogue.title: Packing for the school trip
dialogue.context: Miss Vega helps Mateo, Sofia, Liam and Nadia get ready on the morning of the school trip.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good morning, everyone. Please put your jackets on — it's cold.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I can't find mine. I'm looking for it everywhere!

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: It's on the floor, Mateo. Pick it up and put it on.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Miss, the bus is late. Shall I find out when it's coming?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Yes, please. And turn off your phones when you get on the bus.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I never turn mine off, but I'll try.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Don't give up, Nadia! It's only for the morning.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Mateo, I'll look after your lunch while you get up from the floor.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Thanks! I always get on with you when you're helpful.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Ready? Then take your bags off the floor and let's go!

items.sentence: It's dark in here. Can you ___?
items.why: pronoun goes between turn and on

items.sentence: Nadia ___ with her sister really well.
items.why: get on with = have a good relationship

items.sentence: I'm ___ my keys. Have you seen them?
The shoes are dirty. Please take ___ before you come in.
Mateo wants to ___ who won the game.

practice.instructions: Complete with the phrasal verb in brackets in the correct form. Add it or them where you need to.

items.sentence: It's cold outside. ___ (put on) your coat.
Miss Vega dropped her pen, so Liam ___ (pick up) for her.
Nadia can't find her glasses. She's ___ (look for) them everywhere.
I hate this game and I'm not going to win. I ___ (give up).
I ___ (get on) with all my classmates.
Sofia's aunt always ___ (look after) the dog.
Here are your dirty shoes. Please ___ (take off) before you come in.
Let's ___ (find out) who won the competition.

practice.instructions: Put the words in order. Tap them one by one.

items.answer: I look after my little brother on Saturdays.
Take your shoes off before you come in.
Nadia gets on well with Sofia.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it means the same as the first, using the word given. Use no more than three words.

items.first: Sofia is taking care of her grandmother.
I'm trying to find my phone.
Mateo wants to stop playing the piano.
Nadia is friendly with her teachers.

can_do: I can put it or them in the middle of separable phrasal verbs like turn on, take off and pick up.
I can use look after, look for and get on with correctly, without splitting them.
I can use common phrasal verbs such as put on, give up, find out and get up in everyday sentences.
summary: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word (on, off, up, out) with a new meaning.
With separable ones, a noun can go in the middle or after, but a pronoun always goes in the middle: turn it on.
Inseparable ones are never split: look after it, look for them, get on with him.
Some phrasal verbs need no object: get up, sit down, give up, take off (a plane).
